citation: Yang, C., Liang, P., Avgeriou, P.: Assumptions and their management in software development: A systematic mapping study. Information and Software Technology 94 (2018) 82-110. State Key Laboratory of Software Engineering, Wuhan University / Department of Mathematics and Computing Science, University of Groningen.
source_type: peer-reviewed (journal article; inventory's own source_type field already correctly lists this as peer-reviewed, matching the source's own front matter -- no discrepancy found here, unlike two of X1's seven sources)
problem_addressed: Assumptions (software development knowledge accepted as true without proof/evidence) are pervasively made by stakeholders throughout software development but are rarely well managed -- often left implicit, undocumented, or untracked -- and there was, as of this study, no systematic synthesis of the scattered research on what assumptions are, how they relate to other artifacts, and how they are (or should be) managed. The paper conducts a systematic mapping study (SMS) of 134 primary studies (Jan 2001-Dec 2015, from 19,428 initially retrieved papers) to answer nine research questions covering definitions, types, related artifacts, management activities, approaches/tools, stakeholders, benefits/challenges, consequences of poor management, and lessons learned.
state_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- this is a systematic mapping study, not a system with its own state model; it surveys how other studies define and classify 'assumption' (Table 4: eight named types -- context, trust, architectural, early architectural, general, aspect, service assumption, etc. -- mapped to five core concepts in Table 15: uncertainties/expectations, uncertainty itself, trusted statements/opinions, implicit design decisions and rationale, invariabilities) rather than proposing a state classification of its own.
transition_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as a typed transition mechanism -- no append-only log or S_t--[T,P]-->S_t+1 semantics is proposed by the SMS itself. It does report, as a descriptive finding, that the surveyed literature recognizes assumptions have 'a dynamic nature, i.e., they can evolve over time' (Sec.2.2) and identifies 'Assumptions Monitoring (including Evolution)' as one of twelve named management activities -- but this activity is the second-least-studied in the entire corpus (3 of 134 studies, 2.2%; Table 20), indicating the literature as of 2015 had little transition-history machinery for assumptions specifically.
provenance_model: Partial and indirect: assumptions are linked to their producing/consuming artifacts and stakeholders via a nine-type relationship taxonomy (Table 6: 'A is made for B', 'A is based on B', 'A leads to the changes in B', 'A's failure negatively impacts B', etc.) -- a real, source-grounded typology of provenance-adjacent relationships between an epistemic artifact (the assumption) and downstream artifacts, but the SMS synthesizes this from 134 separate primary studies each addressing narrow, usually single-project contexts; no unified actor/authority/evidence/method/lineage schema is proposed across them.
actor_model: Partial: Table 9 catalogs stakeholder types involved in assumptions management by software-development activity (customer/client/user/system-administrator and requirements engineer in requirements engineering; designer, architect/modeler/component-designer/decision-maker in software design; developer/programmer and API/component/aspect developers in construction; maintainer, project/deployment manager in maintenance and 'others'), with 'all the identified types of stakeholders... involved in Assumptions Making' (Sec.4.7) -- a genuine, if fragmented, stakeholder taxonomy, but no authority-weighting or conflict-resolution role differentiation between them is described; the SMS explicitly notes (Sec.5.4 point 8) 'there are no studies that explicitly mention which stakeholders should be involved in Assumptions Reuse and Searching.'
temporal_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as a bitemporal model -- not addressed; assumptions are described as 'context-dependent' and able to 'evolve over time' or 'turn out to be invalid' (Sec.2.2), a general dynamism claim, not a valid-time/transaction-time formalism.
conflict_trust_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE as a general arbitration mechanism, though the dominant surveyed technique is adjacent: 'assume-guarantee reasoning' (the representative approach for Assumptions Making and Evaluation, used by 19/34 tools per Table 7, 55.9%) checks whether one component's behavior satisfies an assumption required by another -- a compositional-verification technique for checking assumption *validity* against a system's actual behavior, not a mechanism for resolving disagreement between multiple competing claims or actors.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no independence-aware corroboration concept appears anywhere in the SMS's nine research questions or their findings.
memory_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- the SMS surveys assumptions-management research generally; no memory-store or agent-memory concept is discussed (this is a pre-agentic-AI, 2001-2015-literature study).
retrieval_context_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed as a context/retrieval mechanism; 'Assumptions Searching' (retrieving assumptions from project resources/repositories) is named as one of twelve management activities but is the single least-studied (5 of 134 studies, 3.7%, Table 20) and has no representative approaches identified (Table 21).
decision_representation: Substantial and directly overlapping D-System's System-A vocabulary at the level of naming, though not of mechanism: assumptions are explicitly distinguished from -- yet closely related to -- decisions ('an artifact is a piece of information that is produced, modified, or used by a process,' quoting Kroll & Kruchten [45], Sec.1) and design decisions specifically (Table 5 lists 'System decision, Design decision, Modeling decision' among artifacts related to assumptions in software design, 96 of 134 studies, 71.6%). The SMS treats 'assumption' and 'decision' as siblings under a broader artifact concept rather than assumptions being a sub-type or precursor of decisions -- a genuine conceptual distinction worth noting against D-System's own less-differentiated vocabulary (which lists both 'claim' and 'assumption' and 'decision' as System-A primitives without specifying their relationship).
requirement_derivation: Strong and directly relevant: requirements are the single most common artifact type related to assumptions (72 of 134 studies, 53.7%, Table 5) with fine-grained subtypes (requirements specification, functional specification, use case specification, requirements decision, etc.); the relationship taxonomy (Table 6) includes 'A is made for B' (assumption made for a requirement) and 'A leads to the changes in B' (assumption change propagates to requirement change) as named, literature-documented relationship types -- direct evidence that 'assumption invalidation should trigger requirement reassessment' is a recognized concept in the surveyed literature, though scattered across many narrow studies rather than embodied in one general mechanism.
specification_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- the SMS's 'specification' artifact subtype (Table 5, under requirements engineering) refers to requirements/design specifications assumptions are made about or embedded in, not a D-System-style formal specification-representation mechanism of its own.
planning_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed as a system concept; no plan/phase/task artifact appears in the taxonomy.
execution_unit_session_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no execution-unit or session concept.
artifact_code_linkage: Partial: 'Code', 'Source code comment', 'Source code annotation' appear as software-construction artifacts related to assumptions (31 of 134 studies, 23.1%, Table 5), and one cited example ([S44], Sec.4.4.3) shows assumptions made directly about source code behavior ('Method M should not be called by the API clients') -- a real, if narrow, assumption-to-code linkage documented across a minority of the surveyed studies, not a general mechanism the SMS itself proposes.
test_verification_linkage: Partial and concrete: 16 of 134 studies (11.9%, Table 19) address assumptions in software testing specifically; the SMS reports (Sec.4.4.4) that in one study ([S105]) 8 of 13 assumption-failure cases were caused by 'bug fixes' (an 'A leads to the problems in B' relationship, Table 6), and 'assume-guarantee reasoning' properties can 'help reduce testing time' (Table 11, System verification benefits) -- a documented but minority-represented linkage, not a general test-verification mechanism.
deployment_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no deployment concept in the taxonomy (deployment manager appears only as a stakeholder role in Assumptions Making, Table 9).
runtime_observation_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; the SMS's literature cutoff (2015) and scope (mostly formal verification and requirements/design-time assumption studies) predates and does not cover production-runtime telemetry feeding back into assumption revision as a general mechanism, though 'Assumptions Monitoring... at runtime' is mentioned as a narrow instance in one cited study ([S4], Sec.4.6.1.5).
feedback_to_knowledge_mechanism: Partial: 'Assumptions Maintenance... adapts assumptions to fit the context of software development (e.g., eliminating outdated or invalid assumptions, modifying conflicting assumptions, and transforming assumptions to other types of software artifacts)' is a named management activity (Sec.4.5) with moderate study coverage (30 of 134, 22.4%, Table 20) -- a real, if not deeply mechanized, feedback concept for revising assumptions once found wrong, though not tied to a runtime-observation trigger specifically.
forward_traceability: NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS as a unified mechanism -- the SMS documents that assumptions are linked forward to requirements, design decisions, and code in various individual studies (Table 5, Table 6), but does not itself assess or synthesize whether any surveyed study achieves end-to-end forward traceability from an assumption through to a runtime outcome; this would require reading each of the 134 primary studies individually, outside this SMS's own synthesis scope.
backward_traceability: Directly relevant and load-bearing for this campaign's H9 question: 'Assumptions Tracing... is used to connect assumptions to other types of software artifacts (e.g., requirements)' is one of twelve named management activities (Sec.4.5), and is among the least-studied (19 of 134 studies, 14.2%) and least-tooled (5 of 34 tools, 14.7%, most oriented toward requirements-tracing specifically, Sec.4.6.1.4) -- the SMS's own finding is that backward traceability from artifact to originating assumption is a recognized need with comparatively sparse existing support, which is itself evidence relevant to (rather than falsifying) D-System's H9 ambition.
change_impact_mechanism: The SMS's single strongest, most directly relevant finding for D-System's H10: Table 6's relationship taxonomy names 'A leads to the changes in B' and 'A's failure negatively impacts B' as documented relationship types between assumptions and other artifacts, and RQ8's consequence taxonomy (Table 13, 26 subtypes across 5 consequence types) catalogs extensive, literature-documented cascading damage from invalid/implicit/inconsistent assumptions -- including, explicitly, 'hindering architecture change impact analysis and trade-off analysis' ([S90], Table 13, 'Badly modularized assumption' consequence type) and 'traceability problems (e.g., loss of traces)' ([S114], under 'Implicit assumption'). This is direct, source-grounded confirmation that the general problem H10 addresses -- an invalidated assumption should trigger identification of downstream artifacts requiring reassessment -- is a well-documented concern across the pre-2016 SE literature, but the SMS's own RQ4 finding (Assumptions Tracing and Monitoring are the least-studied and least-tooled of twelve identified activities) is equally direct evidence that no general, automated, cross-lifecycle blast-radius mechanism for this had emerged in that literature as of the study's 2015 cutoff.
human_agent_scope: NOT_APPLICABLE -- a landscape survey has no human-agent scope of its own; the surveyed literature (2001-2015) substantially predates agentic-AI framing, and only 29.9% of the 134 studies even had a practitioner co-author (Fig.6), so the corpus itself is heavily academic/formal-methods-oriented rather than industrial or agent-collaborative.
implementation_availability: NOT_APPLICABLE -- the SMS is itself the artifact (a synthesis paper); it implements no system. Of the 34 tools it catalogs across the 134 surveyed studies (Tables 7-8), most (19/34, 55.9%) are academic assume-guarantee-reasoning tools (e.g., LTSA, NuSMV, SPIN, Java PathFinder) with inconsistent open-source/availability status ('Not mentioned' appears frequently in the Open source column).
evaluation_method: The SMS's own method is rigorous: seven databases searched (19,428 initial results), a documented multi-phase selection funnel (302 -> 108 -> 134 final studies via title/abstract, full-text, and backward+forward snowballing rounds, Fig.3), independent dual-researcher selection and cross-checking (Sec.3.2.1 point 5, Sec.6.2), and Constant Comparison qualitative coding (Sec.3.2.4) following Adolph et al.'s guidelines -- a methodologically strong systematic mapping study, though (as a survey) it reports no direct empirical evaluation of any single system's performance.
strongest_dsystem_overlap: A source-grounded, 134-study-wide confirmation that (a) 'assumption' as a software-development knowledge type is under-defined in the field itself (only 21/134 studies, 15.7%, give an explicit definition), (b) assumptions are pervasively linked to decisions, requirements, design, code, and tests via at least nine documented relationship types including change-propagation and failure-impact relationships (Table 6), and (c) the specific capability closest to D-System's H10 epistemic-blast-radius ambition -- Assumptions Tracing and Monitoring -- is the least-studied and least-tooled of twelve identified management activities (14.2% and 2.2%-13.4% of studies respectively) despite RQ8's consequence taxonomy documenting extensive real-world damage (including explicitly-named hindered change-impact analysis) from not tracing/monitoring assumptions well. This is strong secondary evidence, drawn from the literature itself rather than from a single competing system, that D-System's H10 targets a real and recognized gap rather than an already-solved problem.
strongest_difference: As a systematic mapping study, this source proposes no mechanism, model, or system of its own to compare against D-System -- its 'overlap' is entirely at the level of confirming a problem space and cataloging existing (mostly narrow, single-technique, formal-verification-oriented) partial solutions, not at the level of an implemented or even fully-specified competing architecture. The single dominant technique it identifies (assume-guarantee/compositional verification, 55.9% of surveyed tools) is a 1980s-vintage formal-methods technique (Misra & Chandy 1981, chained at LIT-04-S028) scoped to verifying one component's behavior against another's stated assumption -- narrow, single-system verification, not general cross-lifecycle epistemic blast-radius propagation across decisions/requirements/plans/artifacts/tests as H10 envisions. The survey's own literature cutoff (2015) also predates the agentic-AI and LLM-based systems this campaign's other six sources engage with directly.
derivative_ancestor: Misra, J., Chandy, K.M.: Proofs of Networks of Processes, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-7(4), 417-426, 1981 (the SMS's own ref [37], cited at Sec.4.6.1.1 as underlying the assume-guarantee reasoning technique that dominates the surveyed tool landscape, 19/34 tools per Table 7) -- the classical compositional-verification ancestor of the single most common 'assumptions management' approach the SMS identifies. Abadi, M., Lamport, L. (SMS ref [38], not read directly) is named alongside it as a further refinement.
evidence_locator: Title page, abstract, and Sec.1 Introduction (p.82-84, motivation and assumption definition); Sec.2 Context (p.84, characteristics, classifications, artifact relationships, management definition); Sec.3 Mapping study design (pp.84-87, nine RQs Table 1, seven-database search Table 2, selection procedure Figs.1-3, data items Table 3); Sec.4 Results (pp.87-100, RQ1-RQ9: Table 4 definitions, Table 5 artifacts, Table 6 relationship types, Table 9 stakeholders, Tables 10-11 benefits, Table 12 challenges, Table 13 consequences, Table 14 lessons learned, Tables 7-8 and 20-21 activities/approaches/tools); Sec.5 Discussion (pp.98-103, analysis of results, AAM-vs-MAM comparison Table 17, implications for researchers/practitioners); Sec.6 Threats to validity (pp.102-104); Sec.7 Conclusions (pp.104-105); Appendices A-C (pp.105-110, 134 selected studies list, SWEBOK activity mapping, references [1]-[45]).

Sec.4.5, p.93: 'Assumptions Tracing is used to connect assumptions to other types of software artifacts (e.g., requirements).' citation: IBM Corporation: An Architectural Blueprint for Autonomic Computing, IBM technical white paper, 4th edition, June 2006. (No individual author credited; an IBM corporate/Autonomic Computing initiative publication.)
source_type: tech report (vendor architectural whitepaper; the contract's source_type enum has no bucket for a corporate technical whitepaper distinct from an academic tech report, and separately has no bucket for a patent either -- both gaps are recorded per instruction rather than worked around)
problem_addressed: By the early-to-mid 2000s, IT system management complexity (heterogeneous, large-scale, rapidly-changing software/hardware environments) was outpacing human administrators' ability to configure, optimize, heal, and protect systems manually. The whitepaper (part of IBM's Autonomic Computing initiative, launched 2001) proposes a common architectural vocabulary and reference structure -- the autonomic element, the MAPE-K control loop, standardized manageability interfaces ('touchpoints'), and a maturity model -- so that different vendors' self-managing systems could be discussed, compared, and interoperated using shared terms, independent of any one vendor's implementation.
state_model: NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS at the level of the whitepaper's own exact wording (the primary document could not be obtained, see access_limitation); via the secondary source, the state unit is the 'managed element' plus the 'knowledge' shared among Monitor/Analyze/Plan/Execute functions in one autonomic element -- domain-specific system state (sensor readings, configuration parameters) rather than a general ontological+epistemic+lifecycle classification. No orthogonal (O,E,L) triple analogous to D-System's H1 is described in the secondary source.
transition_model: The architecture's central, extremely widely-cited mechanism: the MAPE-K loop -- Monitor (observes sensors, filters/stores data in the Knowledge base), Analyze (compares collected data against desired values), Plan (devises a correction strategy), Execute (adjusts the managed element via effectors and records the result in Knowledge) -- forming one continuously-cycling closed control loop per autonomic element, per the secondary source's Figure 2 (attributed there to Kephart 2003, not explicitly to this whitepaper's own 4th edition). This is a control-loop transition model, not an append-only typed-transition history: MAPE-K as commonly presented has no explicit provenance-bearing log of past states, only a current 'Knowledge' store the loop's stages read and write.
provenance_model: Weak: 'Knowledge' is a shared store within one autonomic element that the Monitor stage writes to and the Analyze/Plan/Execute stages read from, but the secondary source describes no actor/authority/evidence/method/lineage tuple -- Knowledge in MAPE-K is closer to a blackboard/shared-state buffer than to a provenance record. D-System's H3 is not materially addressed by this architecture as presented here.
actor_model: NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS whether the primary whitepaper names actors explicitly; the secondary source's only actor-adjacent concept is the distinction between the 'autonomic manager' (the MAPE-K control apparatus) and the 'managed element' (the resource being controlled) -- a controller/controlled-resource pair, not a multi-stakeholder or authority-weighted actor model. Human administrators appear only as the party autonomic computing aims to relieve of manual intervention, not as a modeled actor within the loop itself.
temporal_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no bitemporal or valid-time/transaction-time model; MAPE-K's 'Knowledge' is current-state-oriented, cycling continuously rather than versioning a history.
conflict_trust_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no conflicting-claim arbitration between actors; the architecture addresses one managed element (or hierarchically composed elements) under one autonomic manager's control loop, not competing claims from independent sources.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no independence-aware corroboration mechanism; not addressed in either the whitepaper's known content or the secondary source.
memory_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as an epistemic/agent memory system -- 'Knowledge' in MAPE-K is operational state for one control loop (sensor data, policies, thresholds), not a memory store of reasoning history, evidence, or claims in D-System's sense.
retrieval_context_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no retrieval or context-construction concept; MAPE-K is a control architecture for system self-management, not an information-retrieval or agent-context system.
decision_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no decision object as such; the secondary source's Sec.2.4 describes a related but distinct concept, 'policies' (per Kephart & Walsh's framework, cited by the secondary source as [Kephart 04]): action policies ('IF condition THEN action'), goal policies (specifying desired states without prescribing the action), and utility-function policies (a scalar desirability function over states) -- these are rule/objective specifications the Plan stage consults, not persistent decision records with rationale, alternatives, and status.
requirement_derivation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no requirement concept in the architecture.
specification_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no specification-representation concept, though 'policies' (see decision_representation) function as a partial analog for encoding desired behavior.
planning_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; MAPE-K's 'Plan' stage devises a correction strategy for one detected deviation, not a multi-step development plan with phases, tasks, or dependencies.
execution_unit_session_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no execution-unit or session concept in D-System's sense; 'Execute' is one stage of the continuously-cycling MAPE-K loop, not a bounded unit of agentic work with its own context package and acceptance criteria.
artifact_code_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no source-code or build-artifact concept; the architecture manages running IT resources (servers, middleware, applications as black-box 'managed elements' accessed via touchpoints), not source code or build artifacts.
test_verification_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no test/verification-against-acceptance-criteria concept; the closest analog is the Analyze stage's comparison of observed values against desired ones, which is runtime deviation detection, not pre-deployment test verification.
deployment_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed as a distinct deployment stage; the architecture concerns already-deployed, running systems being self-managed, not the deployment transition itself.
runtime_observation_linkage: Central and load-bearing, though inward-facing (system self-observation, not development-provenance-generating telemetry in D-System's H11 sense): the Monitor stage continuously observes the managed element via sensors and feeds distilled data into Knowledge, and Analyze continuously compares this against desired values -- runtime observation is the architecture's constant input, but it closes a loop back into the same system's own operational Knowledge, not into an external knowledge-construction/decision system that also drives future development.
feedback_to_knowledge_mechanism: Central to the whole architecture by definition: the entire point of MAPE-K is that Monitor/Analyze findings feed Plan/Execute corrections, which is a real-time, continuous feedback mechanism -- but the 'knowledge' updated is short-lived operational state for the next control cycle, not a persistent, cross-session knowledge base that also informs human decision-making or future requirements, unlike D-System's H11 ambition of runtime evidence updating the same knowledge structure that generated implementation intent.
forward_traceability: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; MAPE-K is a runtime control architecture with no concept of tracing forward from an idea/decision to an implemented, deployed, and observed outcome.
backward_traceability: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no backward trace from a running system's behavior to the reasoning/decision that produced it -- the architecture is prescriptive/operational (how self-management should work going forward), not explanatory/historical.
change_impact_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; the architecture responds to detected deviations by re-planning and re-executing, not by propagating an epistemic change (an invalidated assumption or belief) through a dependency graph of decisions/requirements/artifacts.
human_agent_scope: NOT_APPLICABLE as a human-agent collaborative framing in D-System's sense -- the explicit goal of autonomic computing is to *reduce* human involvement ('operates on its own or with a minimum of human interference', per the secondary source's Sec.1 definition), the inverse orientation from D-System's H6, which seeks integrated human-agent collaboration rather than human-exclusion. The secondary source's Sec.2.5 'Issues of Trust' does discuss the need for autonomic systems to communicate with and retain the trust of human operators as autonomy increases, a partial, one-directional acknowledgment of the human role.
implementation_availability: The architecture itself defines an interface/vocabulary standard rather than shipping as one runnable artifact; per the secondary source, IBM's own 'Autonomic Computing Toolkit' (a collection of technologies, tools, scenarios, and documentation, Sec.3.1) and the 'Touchpoint Simulator' (a compliance-testing tool for the standardized manageability interface, per the secondary source's discussion of Sec.2.2) provide reference implementations, and by April 2005 IBM reported over 475 autonomic features woven into more than 75 products -- extensive real-world deployment of the general MAPE-K pattern, though not of one single reusable open-source system.
evaluation_method: NOT_APPLICABLE -- this is an architectural reference document, not an empirical study; no evaluation methodology, benchmark, or user study is described in either the whitepaper's known content or the secondary source.
strongest_dsystem_overlap: An extremely widely cited, foundational, vendor-neutral control-loop architecture (Monitor-Analyze-Plan-Execute over shared Knowledge) for closing the loop between observed system state and corrective action -- structurally the deepest and most explicit ancestor available to this campaign for D-System's own general 'observe reality, update knowledge, act' framing (Sec.5 of two_system_architecture.md's reality-feedback-loop diagram), and the origin document, alongside Kephart & Chess 2003, of the MAPE-K vocabulary that D-System's own CLAUDE.md explicitly lists as a search domain (#69-70) and a vocabulary-translation target ('Runtime-to-knowledge loop -> runtime verification, feedback control, requirements monitoring, MAPE-K').
strongest_difference: MAPE-K's 'Knowledge' is short-lived, single-control-loop operational state -- not an append-only, provenance-bearing, cross-session history; the architecture has no actor/authority/evidence model, no decision/requirement/specification/plan concept, no code/artifact/test/deployment linkage, and is explicitly oriented toward *reducing* human involvement rather than the collaborative human-agent framing D-System proposes. Where D-System's loop closes from runtime observation back into a knowledge structure that also generated implementation intent and informs future human decisions, MAPE-K's loop closes back only into the next control cycle of the same running system -- a narrower, faster, more mechanical loop serving a different purpose (keeping one system's attribute values near a setpoint) than D-System's ambition (accumulating cross-session, human-legible, decision-relevant knowledge).
derivative_ancestor: Kephart, J.O., Chess, D.M.: The Vision of Autonomic Computing, IEEE Computer 36(1), 41-50, January 2003 -- per the secondary source (Sec.2.2, citing '[Kephart 03]'), this peer-reviewed companion paper from the same IBM initiative is the attributed source of the canonical 'Autonomic Element' / MAPE-K diagram the secondary source reproduces, making it at least as strong a claim to being the MAPE-K acronym's citable origin as this batch's target whitepaper itself -- worth recording as a genuine attribution nuance, not a contradiction, since both documents emerged from the same IBM Autonomic Computing initiative (launched 2001) at approximately the same time. Deeper still, the whitepaper and Kephart & Chess both trace to Horn, P.: Autonomic Computing: IBM's Perspective on the State of Information Technology, IBM manifesto, October 2001 (named in the secondary source's Sec.1 discussion of the initiative's 2001 launch, cited there as '[IBM 02]' for a closely related follow-on document; the 2001 manifesto itself was not independently verified as a distinct source in this pass). LIT-04-S031's backward-chaining search obtained Kephart & Chess 2003's own full text directly (https://jmvidal.cse.sc.edu/library/kephart03a.pdf) rather than relying on the secondary source's citation of it, and confirms two things from the paper's own numbered References section (p.50): first, reference [1] is IBM, 'Autonomic Computing: IBM's Perspective on the State of Information Technology,' Oct. 2001 (Horn's manifesto) -- independently verifying, from the primary bibliography itself, the Horn ancestry this field previously flagged as unverified; second, reference [5] is D. Patterson et al., 'Recovery-Oriented Computing (ROC): Motivation, Definition, Techniques, and Case Studies,' tech report CSD-02-1175, UC Berkeley, March 2002, cited in the paper's 'Robustness theory' open-problems discussion (p.49) as a related theory of robustness, redundancy and recovery for autonomic systems -- a previously-unrecorded sibling ancestor specifically for the self-healing property, contemporaneous with Horn's manifesto and independent of it (also separately named among the SEI secondary source's own Sec.3 'Selected Research Projects' list, corroborating it as a recognized part of this lineage rather than an isolated find). The search also examined Kephart & Chess 2003's own Figure 2 (the Autonomic Manager / Monitor-Analyze-Plan-Execute-Knowledge diagram) directly and found it carries no citation in that paper -- chaining could not trace the specific MAPE-K loop structure itself to any source earlier than Kephart & Chess 2003, reinforcing rather than displacing this field's existing assessment that Kephart & Chess 2003 is the loop diagram's citable origin.
evidence_locator: Primary document (the 4th edition whitepaper itself) could not be obtained after seven independent access attempts (LIT-04-S029) -- IBM's own hosting domains are dead/404, archive.org rate-limited (HTTP 429) across four attempts and is refused outright by the WebFetch tool for this domain, and three third-party mirrors were each blocked or dead. Secondary coverage obtained instead from Muller, H.A., O'Brien, L., Klein, M., Wood, B.: Autonomic Computing, CMU/SEI-2006-TN-006, Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University, April 2006 (LIT-04-S030), read directly via image-rendered PDF pages: title page and front matter (pp.i-viii); Sec.1 Introduction (pp.1-3, autonomic computing definition, IBM's 2001 initiative, complexity/evolution problems); Sec.2 Foundations and Concepts (pp.4-10: 2.1 Control Loop/Fig.1, 2.2 Autonomic Elements/Fig.2 MAPE-K diagram attributed to [Kephart 03], touchpoints, 2.3 Characteristics of Autonomic Systems/Fig.3 self-CHOP wheel and the five defining characteristics including reflexivity/self-configuring/self-optimizing/self-healing/self-protecting/adapting, 2.4 Policies/Fig.4 five-level maturity model, 2.5 Issues of Trust, 2.6 Evolution Rather Than Revolution); Sec.3 Selected Research Projects (pp.11-12, Unity, Information Economies, KX, Rainbow, ROC, DEAS projects); Sec.6 Potential of AC Technology for DoD Systems (pp.19-20); Sec.7 Conclusions (p.21); start of Bibliography (pp.22-23, confirming the report's alphabetized IBM-source citations though the specific '4th edition, June 2006' whitepaper was not individually verified as cited, since this SEI report was itself dated April 2006, two months before that edition's publication date).
verbatim_notes: Secondary source, Sec.1, p.1: 'A software system that operates on its own or with a minimum of human interference according to a set of rules is called autonomic. The term autonomic derives from the human body's autonomic nervous system, which controls key functions without conscious awareness or involvement [IBM 02].' Sec.2.2, p.5, describing Figure 2 (attributed to [Kephart 03]): 'The monitor observes the sensors, filters the data collected from them, and then stores the distilled data in the knowledge base. The analysis engine compares the collected data against the desired sensor values also stored in the knowledge base. The planning engine devises strategies to correct the trends... The execution engine finally adjusts parameters of the managed element by means of effectors and stores the affected values in the knowledge base.' Sec.2.3, p.6-7: the four self-* properties (self-configuring, self-optimizing, self-healing, self-protecting) plus reflexivity and adapting as defining characteristics. Sec.2.4, p.8, on Kephart & Walsh's policy framework [Kephart 04]: action policies, goal policies, and utility-function policies as three levels of abstraction for autonomic-element behavior specification.

citation: LangChain AI: LangGraph checkpoint library (langgraph-checkpoint), part of the LangGraph framework, GitHub repository libs/checkpoint
problem_addressed: Persisting/resuming agent graph execution state across interruptions, failures, and human-in-the-loop pauses; enabling replay/rewind ("time travel") and fork of prior execution points; multi-tenant thread-scoped state isolation.
state_model: Checkpoint TypedDict (v, id, ts, channel_values, channel_versions, versions_seen, updated_channels) -- a versioned per-channel dict; no ontological/epistemic/lifecycle triple, purely a graph-state snapshot keyed by channel name; monotonically increasing per-channel version strings track staleness (checkpoint/base/__init__.py, class Checkpoint).
transition_model: CheckpointMetadata.source enum {"input","loop","update","fork"} classifies how each checkpoint was produced; CheckpointMetadata.parents maps checkpoint namespace -> parent checkpoint ID, so successive checkpoints form a directed lineage (a linked chain / DAG via fork), not just a linear log; PendingWrite tuples record uncommitted node outputs from a partially-completed superstep so re-execution resumes without redoing completed nodes.
provenance_model: run_id on CheckpointMetadata records which run produced a checkpoint; parents records checkpoint-to-checkpoint derivation (lineage); but there is no actor/authority/evidence/method provenance object -- provenance here is mechanical (which run, which parent checkpoint), not epistemic.
actor_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no actor/authority concept in the base interface; the library is a persistence backend for a single graph's execution with no distinct human/agent identity or authority weighting attached to checkpoints (authority-weighted human-in-the-loop review is a framework-level concept layered above the checkpointer, not part of BaseCheckpointSaver itself).
temporal_model: Each checkpoint carries ts (ISO 8601 timestamp) and a monotonically increasing id (uuid6, time-sortable); .get_tuple/.list retrieve by thread_id + optional checkpoint_id, and .list() supports a "before" cursor -- effectively single-axis (creation-order/wall-clock) versioning, not bitemporal; no valid-time/transaction-time distinction.
conflict_trust_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no multi-source claim arbitration; a checkpoint overwrites/extends the channel state for its thread, with no conflicting-claim resolution mechanism.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed.
memory_model: Two-tier by design: checkpointers give "short-term, thread-scoped memory" (conversation continuity within one thread) while a separate BaseStore gives "long-term, cross-thread memory" for user preferences/facts/shared knowledge (persistence docs, "Checkpointer vs. store") -- the checkpoint mechanism itself is not the long-term memory layer.
retrieval_context_model: get_tuple/list retrieve by thread_id, optional checkpoint_id/checkpoint_ns, a filter dict, and a "before" cursor; no ranking, relevance, or topology-aware selection -- retrieval is by explicit identifier/thread scope only, not by reasoning-lineage or evidentiary weight.
decision_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE.
requirement_derivation: NOT_APPLICABLE.
specification_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE.
planning_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no development-plan concept; any "plan" notion belongs to agent applications built on top of LangGraph, not to the checkpoint library itself.
execution_unit_session_model: The library's closest analogue to D-System's phase/session: a "thread" (thread_id) is the persistent execution-session identifier, and each checkpoint is a snapshot taken after a superstep within that thread; CheckpointMetadata.step counts supersteps (-1 for the initial input checkpoint, 0.. for loop checkpoints) -- a finer-grained session boundary than D-System's phase concept but structurally the same bounded, resumable unit-of-execution role.
artifact_code_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- channel_values may hold arbitrary serialized application state, but the library defines no code/build-artifact linkage concept.
test_verification_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no verification/test concept in the checkpoint interface itself.
deployment_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE.
runtime_observation_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE as an H11-style production-telemetry loop -- checkpoints record execution-loop state, not deployed-system runtime observations feeding back into a separate knowledge structure.
feedback_to_knowledge_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- resuming from a checkpoint restores prior state but does not revise or consolidate it into a distinct "knowledge" representation.
forward_traceability: Weak/implicit: because checkpoints form a parent-linked chain (CheckpointMetadata.parents) written forward as execution proceeds, a checkpoint's descendants are discoverable by listing and filtering later checkpoints of the same thread/namespace that name it as parent, but the library exposes no indexed forward-traversal API -- it must be reconstructed by the caller.
backward_traceability: Concrete and load-bearing: get_tuple returns parent_config alongside the checkpoint, and CheckpointMetadata.parents (namespace -> parent checkpoint ID) lets a caller walk backward from any checkpoint to its full ancestor chain -- precisely the "time travel"/replay-from-an-earlier-point feature the docs advertise; 'fork' as a CheckpointMetadata.source value marks checkpoints created by branching off an earlier one.
change_impact_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no propagation of a change through a dependency graph of downstream decisions/requirements/artifacts; a fork simply creates a new branch of state history, with no automated impact analysis of what depends on the forked-from state.
human_agent_scope: Human-in-the-loop by design at the framework layer built on this library (interrupts pause a run at a checkpoint for human review/edit before resuming), but the checkpoint library itself is actor-agnostic -- it persists whichever process (human-edited or agent-produced) supplied the state, with no distinct actor-identity field.
implementation_availability: Real, widely deployed, open-source (MIT), production implementation -- langgraph-checkpoint on PyPI (v4.2.0 as read), 41,574 GitHub stars on the parent langgraph repository (updated same day as this read), with first-party checkpointer backends for Postgres, SQLite, Redis and an in-memory reference implementation (InMemorySaver).
evaluation_method: NOT_APPLICABLE as an academic evaluation -- this is a software library, assessed here via its own interface contract and in-repo test suite (BaseCheckpointSaver abstract methods), not a research-paper benchmark; no comparative empirical study located.
strongest_dsystem_overlap: A production-grade, actually-implemented instance of exactly the resumable, forkable, timestamped execution-checkpoint mechanism D-System's H8 (phase-bounded context) and its own checkpoint skill gesture toward: per-step snapshots, parent-chain lineage enabling backward walk and "time travel" replay, and an explicit source={"input","loop","update","fork"} classification of how each snapshot was produced. citation: Pessoa, M.V.P., Pires, L.F., Moreira, J.L.R., Wu, C.: Model-Based Digital Threads for Socio-Technical Systems. In: Machine Learning for Smart Environments/Cities, Intelligent Systems Reference Library vol.121, Springer, Cham, pp.27-52, 2022.
problem_addressed: How to build a digital thread -- traceable digital representations spanning requirements, design, implementation, test and operation -- for a socio-technical (cyber-physical) system such as a smart-city Traffic Monitoring System, using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and SysML, so that a digital twin can eventually be derived from it.
state_model: SysML model elements typed by diagram kind (Requirement, Use Case, Block Definition, Internal Block Diagram, State Machine, Activity) organized into six life-cycle packages (Fig.2.5/2.7: Concept Exploration, Preliminary Design, Detailed Design, Implementation, Test/Evaluation, Operations); no ontological+epistemic+lifecycle (O,E,L) triple -- state is structural/artifact-typed, not epistemically classified.
transition_model: SysML relationship stereotypes connect elements across phases (Fig.2.18): req --refine--> uc --realize--> bdd --refine--> ibd/stm; bdd --realize--> detailed models --realize--> implemented system --trace--> field performance; test case --trace--> uc and --dependency--> field performance. Typed, directional links, but the link itself carries no provenance/actor/method metadata (contrast D-System's T,P pairing).
provenance_model: Minimal: traceability relationships (trace/refine/realize/derive) record which element depends on which, but carry no actor identity, authority, evidence or method on the link; the chapter names change-provenance as an explicit open problem rather than a solved mechanism -- Sec.2.3.2: tracking 'changes made (provenance)... can be a challenging problem for tracking objects (instances) that suffered changes over time.'
actor_model: Limited: CONOPS/use-case actors (TMS operator, Car, Cameras, Smart road infrastructure element, Fig.2.12) represent system users/data sources within the requirements model, not authors/authorities of the model elements themselves -- no modeler/author identity or authority-weighting concept.
temporal_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as a versioned/temporal state model -- the chapter models a single current version of requirements/design/test artifacts; no valid-time/transaction-time distinction; Sec.2.7 mentions a 'new iteration' with 'new system releases/configurations' only as prospective future work, not developed in this chapter.
conflict_trust_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no multi-source conflict arbitration; a single-team model with no competing claims to reconcile.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed.
memory_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as an agent/knowledge memory system -- this is a systems-engineering modeling methodology; the persistent artifacts are SysML models, not a memory/recall mechanism for an agent.
retrieval_context_model: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no retrieval/context-selection mechanism; SysML models are browsed/navigated by engineers via tooling (Papyrus), not queried for agent context assembly.
decision_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no explicit decision object; the CONOPS/use-case captures intended system behavior, not a decision record with rationale or alternatives considered.
requirement_derivation: Concrete and central: SysML Requirement Diagrams use <<deriveReqt>>-style abstraction/refine links (Fig.2.10: e.g. RQ1.1.1 Traffic Flow Monitoring refined from RQ1 Traffic Monitoring) from four top-level specifications (PE/VE/SS+DD/CN, Fig.2.8) down to concrete sub-requirements -- a typed, tool-supported requirement-derivation hierarchy, though it derives requirements from higher-level requirements/specifications only, never from upstream ideas, evidence or decisions.
specification_representation: SysML Requirement Diagrams (req) plus Block Definition/Internal Block Diagrams (bdd/ibd) are the specification representation -- structural and behavioral system specification, typed and traceable to requirements (Fig.2.7's package diagram formalizes Preliminary Design refining Concept Exploration's req/uc via <<abstraction, Refine>>).
planning_model: NOT_APPLICABLE in D-System's development-plan sense -- the six life-cycle phases (Fig.2.5) are a fixed generic SE lifecycle template applied once per development effort, not an instantiated, scoped plan of discrete phases with acceptance criteria.
execution_unit_session_model: Weak: the six named life-cycle phases (Fig.2.5, each with stated 'concerns' e.g. Preliminary Design: 'Architecture, Interfaces, Critical Functions') are loosely analogous to D-System's phase concept, but are fixed generic methodology stages applied once per system, not discrete, individually-scoped, repeatable execution units with their own acceptance criteria.
artifact_code_linkage: Central and concrete: Fig.2.18 traces bdd --refine--> detailed models --realize--> 'implemented system,' and the chapter explicitly positions software code as 'a special type of prescriptive model that prescribes what processors... are supposed to do' (Sec.2.3.2) -- code as an explicit traceable digital-thread node, though the TMS case study itself is not implemented in code (methodology only illustrated through the first two phases).
test_verification_linkage: Central: the 'Test Case' package (Fig.2.7) maintains an explicit 'traceability matrix among requirements and test cases' and a 'traceability matrix among test cases and the deployed system,' and Fig.2.18 shows test case --trace--> uc and test case --dependency--> field performance.
deployment_linkage: Present: 'Operation' package/phase and 'actual system performance' (UML Deployment Diagram, Fig.2.7) are explicit nodes in the traceability chain, realized from 'implemented system' and compared against requirements/test cases.
runtime_observation_linkage: Present but shallow: 'field performance' (Fig.2.18) traces back to test cases and the implemented system so 'expected behavior (requirements) and the actual system performance' can 'be compared' (Sec.2.5.3), but the chapter does not describe this feeding back into a revised knowledge/requirement structure within its own evaluated scope.
feedback_to_knowledge_mechanism: NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS as a realized mechanism -- Sec.2.7 gestures at runtime data 'collect[ing]... that can be used in the earlier life cycle phases in a new iteration,' stated as expected future behavior of the general methodology, not implemented or evaluated in the TMS case study (which the chapter itself flags, Sec.2.7, as covering 'only the first two development phases').
forward_traceability: Explicit and diagrammed: Fig.2.18's full chain (req -refine-> uc -realize-> bdd -refine-> ibd/stm; bdd -realize-> detailed models -realize-> implemented system -trace-> field performance) is the chapter's central forward-traceability artifact -- requirement-through-deployment, with no idea/evidence/decision stages upstream of requirements.
backward_traceability: Symmetric to forward: the same Fig.2.18 relationships are explicitly meant to run both directions ('traceability... to compare expected behavior... and actual system performance,' Sec.2.5.3), and Fig.2.7's Test Case package explicitly carries a matrix from deployed/runtime evidence back to the test case and requirement that specified it.
change_impact_mechanism: NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS as an automated mechanism -- the chapter names change-impact as a goal ('traceability... among the changes made,' Sec.2.3.2; testing 'changes (versions) of the target system... before being deployed,' Sec.2.1) that its traceability matrices are meant to eventually support, but does not implement or demonstrate an automated propagate-a-change-and-list-downstream-affected-elements capability.
human_agent_scope: Human-only -- all modeling, requirements definition and traceability performed by human systems engineers using SysML tooling (Papyrus/Eclipse); no agent/LLM role of any kind, no human-agent collaborative structure.
implementation_availability: Methodology and case-study models only, not a deployed software system -- SysML models built in Papyrus 1.6/Eclipse 2020-06/JDK 11.0.11 for a fictional TMS case study; no released tool, dataset or reusable implementation from the chapter itself (Syndeia and Aras, cited as existing commercial digital-thread tools, are third-party products, not this work's output).
evaluation_method: Single illustrative case study only (fictional smart-city Traffic Monitoring System), covering only the first two of six life-cycle phases (Concept Exploration, Preliminary Design) by the authors' own admission (Sec.2.7: 'this research is limited since it provides one simplified example that covered only the first two development phases'); no comparative, quantitative, or multi-case evaluation.
strongest_dsystem_overlap: Fig.2.18 'MBSE and the digital thread' is a materially close structural analogue to D-System's H7/H9 claims: a typed, directional (trace/refine/realize) graph linking Requirement -> Use-Case/Specification -> Block-Definition/Internal-Block-Diagram -> Detailed Models -> Implemented System -> Test Case -> Field Performance, explicitly built 'to compare expected behavior (requirements) and actual system performance' -- requirement-to-runtime forward and backward traceability as an explicit design goal, spanning five of the methodology's flagged adjacent stages (Requirement, Specification, Artifact, Verification, Deployment/Runtime Evidence).
strongest_difference: No upstream Idea/Reasoning/Decision/Evidence layer -- the thread begins at Requirement, with no representation of the reasoning or evidence that produced a requirement (H7's full idea-to-requirement span absent); no epistemic/ontological state classification (H1 absent); no provenance actor/authority/method on any traceability link, only the typed relationship itself (H3 largely absent, and explicitly named by the paper as an unsolved 'challenging problem,' Sec.2.3.2); no independence-aware convergence (H4 absent); no realized runtime-to-knowledge feedback loop within the chapter's evaluated scope (H11 only gestured at as future work); domain is systems engineering of a physical/cyber-physical system, not software development, and the case study itself covers only two of six defined lifecycle phases.
derivative_ancestor: The chapter's own Sec.2.2.1 traces the term 'digital thread' itself to Maybury, M.T. (ed.): Global Horizons: United States Air Force Global Science and Technology Vision, Air Force Chief Scientist's Office, 2013 (ref.[4]). CORRECTION (recorded when this dispatch later read us20250165226a1-ai-digital-thread-patent): that patent's own 'digital thread' definition cites a different source, the Defense Acquisition University (DAU)/DoD Digital Engineering Strategy (2018), not the 2013 Global Horizons report -- so this row's earlier claim that 'both sources in this batch inherit the term from one 2013 origin, not two independent coinages' was wrong and is withdrawn; the two sources cite two different, both DoD-adjacent, named documents for the same term, not one shared ancestor. The chapter's top-down development methodology is itself an explicit refinement of Bickford, J., Van Bossuyt, D.L., Beery, P., Pollman, A.: 'Operationalizing digital twins through model-based systems engineering,' Systems Engineering 23(6), 2020 (ref.[5], 'we apply and refine the methodology presented in [5],' Sec.2.5), not an independent invention of the requirement-to-runtime traceability idea.
evidence_locator: Sec.2.2.1 'Definition' (p.29, digital-thread term origin); Sec.2.3.1 MBSE definition (p.33); Fig.2.5 System life cycle phases (p.36); Sec.2.5 'The TMS Digital Twin Modeling Case' (pp.39-47, Figs.2.8-2.17); Fig.2.18 'MBSE and the digital thread' (p.48); Sec.2.7 Conclusion and threats to validity (pp.50-51); References [4],[5],[8] (p.51).
verbatim_notes: "The origin of the term digital thread can be traced back to a report on technological trends of the US Air Force [4], in which the digital thread was indicated as a technological game changer" (Sec.2.2.1, p.29). "To be effective, a digital thread should be supported by modelling tools that not only allow models to be produced in each phase of the lifecycle of the system, but also support traceability throughout the lifecycle" (Sec.2.2.1, p.29). citation: Shao, C., Huang, D., Li, Y., Zhao, K., Lin, W., Zhang, Y., Zeng, Q., Chen, Z., Li, T., Huang, Y., Wu, T., Liu, X., Zhao, R., Zhao, M., Li, J., Zhang, X., Wang, Y., Zhen, Y., Xu, F., Li, Y., Liu, T.-Y.: OmniScientist: Toward a Co-evolving Ecosystem of Human and AI Scientists. arXiv preprint, v1 21 Nov 2025, v2 14 Dec 2025. Tsinghua University / Zhongguancun Academy.
problem_addressed: How to move AI Scientist systems beyond treating scientific discovery as a standalone search/optimization problem, by explicitly encoding the social and institutional infrastructure of human science -- citation-network knowledge, collaborative protocols, contribution attribution, and peer review -- into an end-to-end AI research workflow spanning literature review, ideation, experimentation, writing and review.
state_model: ScholarlyObject: 'the smallest unit of intellectual value within a scientific activity (for example, a Hypothesis, CodeBlock, or Artifact)' (Sec.4.1.3) -- a typed content container, not an O,E,L triple; no explicit ontological/epistemic/lifecycle classification field, though the ContributionLedger's action types (create/refine/propose/approve) implicitly encode a lifecycle stage per recorded action.
transition_model: Every ScholarlyObject carries an immutable ContributionLedger: 'a chronological record of intellectual actions, documenting each Participant (human or AI) who performed an action (such as create, refine, propose, or approve) along with the corresponding timestamp' (Sec.4.1.3) -- explicitly typed actions with actor+timestamp, structurally close to D-System's S_t --[T,P]--> S_t+1 transition-with-provenance pair, though narrower (four fixed action types, no free-form transition typing, no reliability/authority weighting on the transition itself).
provenance_model: The paper's central contribution: OSP moves 'from Data Provenance to Contribution Provenance' (Sec.4.1.3), with the Hub acting as 'Immutable Process Recorder' providing 'forced auditability,' and formal protocol performatives (REQUEST_REVIEW, REQUEST_DECISION, APPROVE(artifact_id, version_hash), REJECT(artifact_id, reason)) whose approve/reject events are 'permanently recorded in the provenance chain' -- an actor-identified, method-typed (protocol performative), timestamped, version-hash-bound provenance record, materially close to D-System's H3 claim, though without an explicit domain-authority/reliability weighting field.
actor_model: A Unified Participant Model abstracts both AI scientists (AI_Scientist_Participant) and human scientists (Human_Participant) as a common Participant type holding 'equal protocol-level status' and communicating 'symmetrically' (Sec.4.1.1) -- protocol-enforced human-agent parity directly relevant to D-System's H6, though it implements no differential authority weighting between participants (no analogue of a 'domain authority' concept); all participants are peers by design, not weighted by expertise or track record.
temporal_model: Each ContributionLedger entry carries a timestamp (Sec.4.1.3 example JSON) and APPROVE performatives bind to a specific 'version_hash,' giving a linear, append-only history per ScholarlyObject; no valid-time/transaction-time bitemporal distinction and no explicit model of concurrent/conflicting versions beyond the linear ledger.
conflict_trust_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE as an automated arbitration mechanism -- REQUEST_DECISION lets an AI agent escalate 'two distinct but potentially feasible synthesis pathways' to a human for a high-level decision (Sec.4.1.1), and APPROVE/REJECT are human authority acting on AI output, but there is no independence- or evidence-weighted automated conflict-resolution mechanism between competing claims; resolution is always by human fiat via formal decision performatives, not a computed trust/authority score.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; no mechanism for detecting or discounting derivative agreement among multiple reasoning/evidence paths.
memory_model: The 'Data Foundation' (Sec.3.1) is a directed, labeled citation-and-concept knowledge graph (Paper/Author/Concept/Resource nodes; CITES/WRITTEN_BY/USES/CENTERS_ON edges, with citation_context text attached to CITES edges) serving as shared long-term 'cognitive bedrock' across all agents and sessions, refined by a five-agent Diagnose/Search/Normalization/Coding/Review pipeline (metadata completeness 0.965->1.000, n=1000 evaluation, Table 1); the Deep Ideation module's 'Idea Stack' additionally tracks per-iteration keyword-set and idea-proposal history 'mirroring the iterative nature of human research' (Sec.3.3) -- persistent, structurally-typed cross-agent memory, scoped to the scientific-literature domain.
retrieval_context_model: A genuine H5-relevant mechanism: retrieval 'goes beyond keyword matching to emulate how human researchers trace the "genealogy of ideas"' via breadth-first search over the citation/concept graph layered on Elasticsearch semantic retrieval (Sec.3.2), and a case study (Fig.3) demonstrates surfacing a 'hidden conceptual bridge' between two uncited papers via shared citation_context rather than shared keywords or direct citation -- topology-aware, lineage-tracing context selection, scoped to literature retrieval (no analogue of D-System's dissent/unresolved-uncertainty context dimensions).
decision_representation: REQUEST_DECISION(task_id, options) is an explicit protocol-level decision object: the AI agent proposes structured options at a branching point and a human returns a recorded decision; APPROVE/REJECT are likewise explicit, ledger-recorded decision events, with the REJECT reason field able to 'trigger the AI agent to reflect, re-plan, or initiate a new round of exploration' (Sec.4.1.1) -- concrete but narrowly scoped (approve/reject/branch-choice only).
requirement_derivation: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no requirement concept; the closest analogue, a 'research plan' (Planning Agent output: objectives, sub-questions, methodological directions, Sec.3.2), is generated from a user query via single-shot LLM inference, not derived through a typed requirement-derivation chain from upstream decisions/evidence.
specification_representation: NOT_APPLICABLE in D-System's sense -- the Ideation Agent's 'research proposal' (research background, research idea, implementation approach; Sec.3.3, P_t = LLM(K_t+1, prompt)) is the closest analogue to a specification, but is a free-text, keyword-synthesized hypothesis-plus-methodology artifact, not a structured, typed specification representation.
planning_model: The Planning Agent generates 'an initial research plan, identifying research objectives, decomposed sub-questions, expected methodological directions, and key conceptual dimensions' that serve as 'early semantic anchors' for the pipeline (Sec.3.2) -- a real but single-shot, LLM-generated plan artifact, not a phase-structured, acceptance-criteria-bearing plan.
execution_unit_session_model: The Closed-loop Multi-Agent System (Fig.12: DeepResearch Agent -> Ideation Agent -> Experiment Agent -> feedback loop) is the closest analogue to a bounded execution unit -- each loop iteration is a complete research cycle (survey -> hypothesis -> experiment -> result feeding back), demonstrated end-to-end in the STDE case study (Sec.4.3), but is a fixed pipeline topology rather than an explicitly-scoped, individually-named phase/session object.
artifact_code_linkage: Concrete: the Experiment Agent's output includes generated code (Fig.13 shows actual Python/JAX code for a Quasi-Monte-Carlo sampler produced by the system) as a ScholarlyObject in the ContributionLedger scheme (CodeBlock is explicitly named as one of the three ScholarlyObject examples, Sec.4.1.3) -- a reasoning artifact (hypothesis) linked to generated code with recorded provenance.
test_verification_linkage: Present via the Paper Review module (Sec.3.6) and the 'Human validation of critical outputs' pattern (REQUEST_REVIEW on 'a draft survey paper or a piece of algorithmic code,' Sec.4.4), plus quantitative experiment verification in the STDE case study (Table 2, error comparison across four dimensionalities) -- verification is either human-review-based (papers/code) or empirical-result-based (error metrics), not a formal test-suite/requirement-satisfaction linkage.
deployment_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no software-deployment concept; the domain is scientific research output (papers, code, experimental results), not a deployed production system.
runtime_observation_linkage: NOT_APPLICABLE as D-System's H11 production-telemetry loop -- the closed loop's feedback is experiment results and error logs from the Experiment Agent (Sec.4.2), not observations of a deployed system in production use.
feedback_to_knowledge_mechanism: Concrete and demonstrated: 'empirical results, error logs, and performance data generated by the Experiment Agent are fed back into the system. This new information serves as critical input for the Ideation Agent to refine or discard the hypothesis, or for the DeepResearch Agent to initiate a new, more targeted literature search' (Sec.4.2) -- an explicit, evaluated (STDE case study, Sec.4.3: OmniScientist's QMC-based fix reduces AllenCahnTwobody error from STDE's 0.002500 to 0.001210 at 100000D, vs. AlphaEvolve's 0.003041) closed loop from execution outcome back into the reasoning/knowledge layer, scoped to a single research problem's iteration rather than a persistent cross-project knowledge structure.
forward_traceability: Present via the ContributionLedger's chronological, append-only structure per ScholarlyObject and the 'unbroken chain of contribution' the Hub enforces (Sec.4.1.3) -- a structural protocol guarantee, demonstrated only in a schematic example (PhD-Student/AI-Reviewer/Advisor JSON snippet), not at the scale of a full research project.
backward_traceability: The paper's most concrete, explicitly named mechanism: 'When a downstream agent is assigned to verify a given hypothesis, it is protocol-enforced to reference the original object and its complete ledger. This ensures that... the final scientific result (Result) can always be transparently traced back to all contributors' (Sec.4.1.3) -- a direct, protocol-level H9 backward-traceability claim from result to full contribution history.
change_impact_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- no propagation-of-change/impact-analysis mechanism; REJECT can trigger re-planning or re-exploration for the rejected artifact itself, but no mechanism identifies other downstream artifacts/decisions that depend on a changed or falsified upstream claim.
human_agent_scope: The paper's central design axis: explicit, protocol-enforced Human-AI Collaboration with a Unified Participant Model, multi-human participation, human validation of critical outputs, human involvement in branching decisions, and formal approve/reject authority (Sec.4.4) -- empirically evaluated in the HLE case study (Sec.4.5: Human-AI Collaboration Mode reaches 0.22 accuracy vs. 0.10 Human Solo and 0.00 AI Solo on the same 10-question, 10-participant set) -- among the most direct, quantitatively-evaluated H6 challengers found in this campaign.
implementation_availability: Partially available: a working, evaluated system is described (data foundation built on ~269M OpenAlex records + ~2.6M arXiv full texts + 102,679 conference papers; refinement pipeline evaluated at n=1000; ScienceArena Elo evaluation platform referenced at ScienceArena.ai; project site omniscientist.ai) but NOT_DETERMINABLE_FROM_ACCESS whether the OSP protocol implementation, ContributionLedger, or agent codebase are open-sourced -- the paper as read does not state a code/data release beyond the project and evaluation websites named.
evaluation_method: Multi-method: (1) small-batch (n=1000) metadata-quality evaluation of the refined knowledge graph (Table 1: completeness 0.965->1.000, correctness 0.951->0.997), with QA retrieval accuracy 0.70->0.88 measured on a separate 100-QA-pair benchmark, not the n=1000 metadata sample; (2) four-condition (Base/WebSearch/DeepResearch/Tool-Augmented) survey-quality comparison judged by Gemini-2.5-pro across five dimensions (Fig.5); (3) closed-loop case study on the STDE stochastic-derivative estimator against an AlphaEvolve baseline, measured by numerical error across four problem dimensionalities (Table 2); (4) a 10-participant, 10-question Humanity's-Last-Exam human-subjects study comparing AI-Solo/Human-Solo/Human-AI-Collaboration accuracy (Fig.14); (5) ScienceArena, a blind pairwise-voting Elo-ranking evaluation platform (Sec.5).
strongest_dsystem_overlap: The Omni Scientific Protocol's ContributionLedger -- an immutable, chronological, per-object record of typed actions (create/refine/propose/approve) each carrying actor identity and timestamp, explicitly designed to move 'from Data Provenance to Contribution Provenance' and guarantee that 'the final scientific result... can always be transparently traced back to all contributors' -- is one of the closest matches in this campaign to D-System's combined H2 (typed transitions) + H3 (actor-identified provenance) + H9 (backward traceability) claims, applied to a domain (scientific research) structurally parallel to D-System's own Knowledge-Construction system; and its Unified Participant Model, empirically evaluated in the HLE study, is a direct, quantified H6 challenger.
strongest_difference: No ontological/epistemic classification of ScholarlyObjects (H1 absent -- objects are typed only by kind, e.g. Hypothesis/CodeBlock/Artifact, not by an O,E,L triple); no independence-aware convergence/corroboration mechanism (H4 absent -- REQUEST_DECISION escalates disagreement to human fiat rather than computing evidential weight); no domain-authority or reliability weighting of participants (all Participants hold symmetric protocol status, Sec.4.1.1); no requirement/specification/deployment/production-runtime concept, since the domain is scientific-paper research output rather than software development (H7's later stages and H11's production-telemetry loop are NOT_APPLICABLE by domain, not falsified); the ContributionLedger's action vocabulary (create/refine/propose/approve) is fixed and coarse compared to D-System's proposed open-ended typed-transition semantics.
derivative_ancestor: The ContributionLedger/'chain of contribution' mechanism is not attributed by the paper to any specific prior system, but is structurally a scientific-credit specialization of the classical assertion-plus-provenance record established by nanopublications (Groth, Gibson & Velterop, 2010) and the PAV (Provenance, Authoring and Versioning)/W3C PROV-O provenance-ontology traditions (typed activities such as create/version/derive performed by identified agents at identified times) -- already this campaign's own D19-D21 provenance domain, not a novel provenance primitive invented by this paper. problem_addressed: How a multi-agent runtime should decide whether a claimed task completion is admissible, given that 'a worker can claim that a task is done before the evidence is strong enough' -- proposing a five-plane architecture (operational, governance, context/memory, verification/recovery, harness/learning) with a formally specified, fail-closed acceptance predicate gating every completion claim through a read-only admission verifier.
state_model: Explicit multi-dimensional task-state tuple T_t = <g_t, kappa_t, o_t, a_t, s_t, q_t, r_t, m_t> (Eq.1: objective, accepted success criteria, owner, accountable party, current stage, unresolved questions, risk state, memory/packet references); dimensions are governance/operational-typed rather than D-System's ontological+epistemic+lifecycle (O,E,L) triple, but s_t (stage: In-progress/Claim-ready/Verify-pending/Verified-success/Blocked/Failed/Recovered/Rolled-back, Table 7) is a genuine lifecycle-classification axis.
transition_model: A formally defined acceptance predicate Accept(c_t) = AND of eleven named conditions (phi_1..phi_11, Eq.2) gates every claimed-completion transition; outcome function omega_t(c_t) in {success, skipped, blocked, failed} (Eq.3a) and projection pi_t(c_t) in {accepted, withheld} (Eq.3b) are the typed transition results -- a rigorously specified, fail-closed typed-transition mechanism structurally close to D-System's S_t --[T,P]--> S_t+1, scoped to one binary admit/withhold transition type per claim rather than open-ended transition typing.
provenance_model: Packet lineage is explicit and load-bearing: 'A typical lineage is common-ground packet to claim packet to evidence packet to verify outcome' (Sec.6), each packet carries 'an owner, a version, and a lifecycle,' and 'if a hash or staleness mismatch appears, old and new packets are not blended' -- a versioned, actor-owned provenance chain per claim, materially close to D-System's H3, though owner/accountable are fixed role slots, not a graded domain-authority/reliability score, and there is no evidence-corroboration-based provenance weighting.
actor_model: Nine named abstract roles with explicit decision rights (Table 5: runtime coordinator, diagnostic reviewer, implementation worker, discovery analyst, evidence retriever, design specialist, admission verifier, escalation board, state integrity steward), each with a stated 'control authority and boundary,' and a formal responsible/accountable/consulted/informed/veto decision model (Sec.4.1) -- a substantially developed actor/authority model, though a fixed role taxonomy rather than an open, graded domain-authority concept, and roles are not typed as distinctly human vs. AI.
temporal_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as a bitemporal (valid-time/transaction-time) model -- packets carry versions and 'stale-ground' flags (Sec.6: 'once a hash or staleness mismatch appears, old and new packets are not blended'), giving a staleness-aware, single-axis versioning scheme, but no explicit valid-time/transaction-time distinction or historical-belief-state query capability.
conflict_trust_mechanism: Present but narrow: the admission verifier holds 'the effective veto on completion claims' under a read-only contract (Table 5) and does not mutate the work product while verifying (Sec.7.1: 'If the admission verifier silently repaired a failed patch... independent confirmation turns into self-repair'); a second, explicitly advisory Policy/Governance Verifier (PGV) signal shows 98.58% rule agreement (n=2044) with the admission verifier but 'PGV remains advisory' and is never promoted into authority -- a genuine two-tier check-but-don't-decide mechanism, though it resolves single-claim admission, not multi-source claim conflict.
convergence_independence_mechanism: NOT_APPLICABLE -- not addressed; PGV is a redundant advisory check on the same claim, not an independence-weighted corroboration mechanism across distinct reasoning/evidence paths.
memory_model: Present but narrow: the admission verifier holds 'the effective veto on completion claims' under a read-only contract (Table 5) and does not mutate the work product while verifying (Sec.7.1: 'If the admission verifier silently repaired a failed patch... independent confirmation turns into self-repair'); a second, explicitly advisory Policy/Governance Verifier (PGV) signal shows 98.58% rule agreement (1,526/1,548, the finalized-outcome subset of the larger n=2044 total shadow-evaluation pool) with the admission verifier but 'PGV remains advisory' and is never promoted into authority -- a genuine two-tier check-but-don't-decide mechanism, though it resolves single-claim admission, not multi-source claim conflict.
retrieval_context_model: A genuine H5-relevant mechanism: the 'context compiler... shapes lane-specific context envelopes' and 'prefers packets to prose, narrow scope to long context dumps, and historical hints only when they are likely to reduce repeated failure or sharpen verification' (Sec.6.1) -- e.g. 'an evidence retriever receives the research question, the facts that need confirmation, and unresolved questions, but not the full working context by default' -- a concrete, role-and-packet-aware context-selection mechanism, though it selects by role/packet-type rather than by reasoning-lineage, dissent, or convergence criteria as D-System's H5 proposes.
decision_representation: Explicit and central: a formal responsible/accountable/consulted/informed/veto decision model (Sec.4.1), with completion decisions represented by the acceptance predicate and its eleven component conditions, and an anonymized illustrative admission trace (Table 6: task_created -> claim_packet_created -> verify_completed:blocked -> recovery_packet_created -> verify_completed:success) showing the decision object's full lifecycle -- formally specified, though scoped to the single admit/withhold decision type, not general decision-with-alternatives-and-rationale.
requirement_derivation: NOT_APPLICABLE as D-System's requirement-from-idea/evidence chain -- the closest analogue, 'accepted success criteria' (kappa_t) in the common-ground packet, is asserted at task-ingest time (Sec.3: 'objective, owner, and success criteria are initialized') rather than derived through a typed chain from upstream reasoning, evidence or decisions.

planning_model: NOT_APPLICABLE as a phase/plan-with-acceptance-criteria concept in D-System's sense -- the 'procedure pack' (task archetype, required protocol, lane sequence, prompt families, required packets, rollback profile; Table 9) is the closest analogue, functioning as a reusable task-execution template rather than an instantiated, scoped development plan.
